The Blacksaddled coralgrouper (Plectropomus laevis) reaches a maximum total length of 125 cm [Li = 125 cm], making it one of the larger serranid species inhabiting Indo-Pacific coral reef systems. Field surveys conducted around the Great Barrier Reef indicate that individuals attain a wet weight at puberty of 2762 g [Wwp = 2762 g], a milestone that typically coincides with the onset of gonadal recrudescence observed during the austral summer spawning season. This body mass at sexual maturation is consistent with the allometric scaling relationship derived from length-weight regressions for this species. The total length at puberty has been estimated at 60 cm [Lp = 60 cm], representing approximately half the asymptotic length, a pattern commonly reported among long-lived grouper species where reproductive investment is deferred until substantial somatic growth has been completed. Otolith-based aging studies further confirm that the transition from the juvenile to the adult phase is not strictly size-dependent but also modulated by local environmental conditions and population density. Comparative analyses with congeneric species such as Plectropomus leopardus suggest that the relatively large size at puberty in P. laevis may confer a fecundity advantage, as larger females produce disproportionately more oocytes per spawning event.

Embryonic development in Plectropomus laevis proceeds rapidly under the stable thermal conditions typical of tropical reef environments. At a water temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval from egg fertilization to hatching, is only 5 days [ab = 5 days]. This short incubation period is characteristic of pelagic-spawning serranids, whose small, buoyant eggs are vulnerable to predation and require rapid embryogenesis. The wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00045 g [Wwb = approximately 0.00045 g], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 0.95 millimeters using the geometric formula for a prolate spheroid. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days post-hatching. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after mouth opening, typically between days three and five. The small initial body mass reflects the energetic constraints of producing thousands of pelagic eggs per female, a classic r-selected strategy that compensates for high larval mortality rates in the planktonic environment. Mortality during the early larval phase is substantial, with predation and starvation being the primary sources of loss.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) is 4.5% [GSI = 4.5%], measured at a water temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. During the spawning season, females may release multiple batches of pelagic eggs over several weeks, spreading reproductive effort across time. Histological examination of ovarian tissue reveals asynchronous oocyte development, with oocytes at various stages of vitellogenesis present simultaneously, enabling serial spawning. The energetic cost of repeated gamete production is partially offset by the warm ambient temperature (27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]), which supports high metabolic rates and efficient food assimilation. Field observations indicate that spawning aggregations form at specific reef promontories during the new moon phase. This pattern stands in contrast to semelparous species that invest a much larger fraction of body mass into a single reproductive bout.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult Blacksaddled coralgrouper is approximately 26094 g [Wwi = approximately 26094 g], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species using data collected across multiple locations in the Coral Sea. This large asymptotic body mass, corresponding to the maximum total length of 125 cm, places Plectropomus laevis among the apex predators within its reef habitat, where it preys primarily on small fishes and crustaceans. Growth parameters estimated from tag-recapture studies suggest that individuals approach this asymptotic weight gradually, with growth rates slowing markedly after the onset of sexual maturity. The length-weight relationship used, following the general form W = aL^b, yields an exponent of approximately 3.06, indicating slightly positively allometric growth, where body depth increases somewhat faster than length. This robust body shape is advantageous for ambush predation in structurally complex reef environments. Maximum recorded longevity in the wild, under the prevailing thermal regime of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], is approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years], a lifespan that is typical for large, slow-growing serranids with delayed reproduction. Long-term monitoring of tagged individuals on the Great Barrier Reef has confirmed that some adults survive for at least two decades, though fishing pressure has reduced the average age of the population in exploited areas.

Comparative physiological studies of Plectropomus laevis have shed light on the interplay between body size, temperature, and life-history scheduling. The maximum lifespan of approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days] at 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C] positions this grouper among the longer-lived members of the Epinephelinae subfamily, a clade known for its generally slow life-history pace. This exceptional longevity, coupled with the relatively late attainment of a total length of 60 cm at puberty [Lp = 60 cm at puberty], reflects a life-history strategy geared toward sustained reproductive output over many years. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 2762 g [Wwp = 2762 g] represents only about ten percent of the ultimate wet weight of 26094 g [Wwi = 26094 g], indicating that females begin reproducing at a relatively small fraction of their maximum size. This early onset of reproduction, despite the modest initial mass, suggests that although Plectropomus laevis is long-lived, it does not postpone first breeding as extremely as some other large reef fishes. The small birth mass of 0.00045 g [Wwb = 0.00045 g] and the rapid development time of 5 days [ab = 5 days] from fertilization to hatching at 27.6 °C underscore the high fecundity required to offset pelagic larval mortality at a temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. Collectively, these traits paint a portrait of a species well adapted to stable tropical reef environments, where moderate but consistent reproductive effort over a long adult lifespan sustains population stability.
